feedback: If a learner picks gamma 'because it carries the most energy': separate the ideas — energy/frequency vary across the spectrum, but vacuum speed does not; light from all stars arrives on time regardless of colour.

If a learner picks radio 'because its wavelength is longer': apply v = fλ with v = c — a long wavelength simply pairs with a low frequency; the product (speed) is identical, so longer does not mean faster.

If a learner says the vacuum stops or slows the waves, or that they need a medium: contrast with sound — EM waves are self-propagating electric/magnetic oscillations that cross empty space, which is exactly why we see the Sun and stars while space is silent.

Full-credit response: says 'together', explains that all EM waves share one vacuum speed independent of frequency/energy, infers that radio must have the much longer wavelength, and keeps 'same speed' distinct from 'different energy/hazard'.
activities.intendedInsight: Speed in a vacuum is the same for all EM waves and is independent of frequency, energy and wavelength; what varies along the spectrum is frequency/energy (hence hazard) and wavelength — and EM waves, unlike sound, need no medium.
learnerActions: Consider: a distant exploding star emits a burst of radio waves AND a burst of gamma rays at the very same instant, both crossing empty space to Earth. Decide which arrives first — radio, gamma, or together — and write WHY.
State the defining rule in your own words: all EM waves travel at 3×10⁸ m/s in a vacuum, regardless of frequency or energy.
Given equal speed but very different frequencies for radio and gamma, work out what MUST differ about their wavelengths (use v = fλ with v fixed at c).
Explain, using the energy/ionisation chain, why gamma is far more dangerous to living tissue than radio even though both travel at the same speed.
Explain why the Sun is silent in space yet blazes with light — what that shows about EM waves versus sound.
activities.title: Same speed, different energy: the star-burst reasoning task
